title: Chomsky's Grammar Hierarchy and Why Parsers Work the Way They Do (1956)
explainer: Linguist Noam Chomsky classified grammars into four nested levels of expressive power in 1956, work aimed at describing natural language, not computers. It turned out that the second-most-restrictive level, context-free grammars, is exactly expressive enough to describe the syntax of most programming languages while staying efficient to parse, which is why BNF-style grammars and tools like parser generators are built on it. When you design a language's grammar, you're choosing a point on a hierarchy a linguist drew up for an entirely different purpose.

title: John Backus and FORTRAN, the First Widely-Used High-Level Language (1957)
explainer: John Backus proposed to IBM management in 1953 that programmers could write in math-like notation and have a machine translate it into efficient code, an idea many colleagues doubted was possible without losing performance. His team's FORTRAN compiler, shipped in 1957, proved a high-level language could compile to code nearly as fast as hand-written assembly, the argument every language implementer has had to win ever since. The lesson's concerns about compilation strategy and performance trade-offs begin with the problem Backus's team solved first.
